issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette: Mrs. Oluwakemi, a 74-year-old African woman and an agricultural worker, has been living with the aftermath of a traumatic rape that occurred several years ago. The trauma continues to manifest in her life through various triggers and maladaptive strategies, creating a complex and distressing cycle. On anniversaries of the event, Mrs. Oluwakemi is particularly affected by the smell of soil and silence-both potent reminders of the day she was attacked while working alone in the fields. The anniversary brings back vivid memories of that silent, dark moment when her attacker appeared from nowhere. She recalls feeling overwhelmed by the earthy scent that filled the air as she tried to escape. These triggers have led Mrs. Oluwakemi to adopt several maladaptive strategies to cope with the overwhelming feelings of fear and distress they evoke. To manage these reactions, she forces herself to think only positive thoughts, believing that focusing on positivity will shield her from reliving those harrowing moments. She also avoids circumstances that remind her of the event, such as being in the dark or any situation where she might be alone outdoors, which has significantly limited her ability to work and engage with others. The anniversary marks a day when she isolates herself completely, avoiding all physical contact because it triggers painful memories of what happened. This isolation deepens her sense that life is not worth living anymore. She feels ashamed of what happened to her body and perceives herself as contaminated by the event. These negative appraisals lead her to believe that she must avoid any situation that might trigger these feelings again, reinforcing her maladaptive strategies. Her negative appraisals also amplify her sensitivity to triggers. For instance, when she smells soil or experiences silence, her belief that life is not worth living intensifies her distress and fear, making the memories more vivid and painful. This vicious cycle has made it increasingly difficult for her to engage in activities she once enjoyed, such as working in the fields with her colleagues. Mrs. Oluwakemi's forced positive reframing often fails to alleviate her deep-seated feelings of shame and contamination. Instead, these strategies often backfire, leading her to feel even more trapped by the trauma. She believes that if she allows herself to think negatively or acknowledge the pain, it will only make things worse, so she pushes those thoughts away. This cycle has taken a toll on her relationship with her partner. While he tries to support her, Mrs. Oluwakemi's avoidance and isolating behaviors have created a significant distance between them. Her fear of being touched by anyone, including her partner, has led to frequent arguments and misunderstanding. What finally brought Mrs. Oluwakemi to seek help was the realization that she could no longer maintain this facade of normalcy. She began to recognize how her maladaptive strategies were not helping but instead exacerbating her sense of worthlessness and isolation. Despite her deep-seated fear, she is most hopeful for a way to find peace with her past and reclaim some control over her life without being constantly haunted by the memories. In therapy, Mrs. Oluwakemi hopes to address the specific triggers that are so potent in her daily life-soil smells, silence, anniversaries-and to find healthier ways of coping that do not isolate or contaminate her further. She is most afraid of feeling trapped in a cycle of negative beliefs and maladaptive behaviors but is eager for support to break free from this pattern.
